questions.question: "Marginalised" in economics means:
options: Pushed to the edge of economic life — excluded from ownership, employment, skills, credit and decision-making

questions.question: Disadvantage persists after the laws are repealed because:
options: The laws were never actually changed
It transmits across generations — through assets, education, networks and address

questions.question: Rural communities were marginalised principally through:
options: Areas deliberately starved of infrastructure and investment — the spatial pattern behind today's geography of unemployment

questions.question: The "compounding" point means:
options: Marginalisation ended simultaneously for all groups
The categories OVERLAP — a young rural Black woman with a disability faces one compounded exclusion, not five separate ones

subtopics.title: Redress Through the Factors of Production

questions.question: Land reform's three programmes are:
options: RESTITUTION (return or compensation for post-1913 dispossession), REDISTRIBUTION (transfer to those without access), TENURE reform (securing insecure occupation)

questions.question: "Land without support fails" means redress in this factor requires:
options: Finance, training, equipment and market access alongside the title deed — or the transfer produces neither livelihood nor output

questions.question: Employment equity deliberately targets management and skilled occupations because:
options: That is where exclusion was sharpest — and where decisions get made
The law only applies to senior staff

questions.question: Redress in the CAPITAL factor addresses:
options: WHO OWNS productive capital — ownership stakes, management control, enterprise and supplier development, preferential procurement — plus credit access for those without collateral

questions.question: Labour legislation is itself democratisation because:
options: The rights to organise, bargain and be consulted convert workers from subjects of decisions into parties to them
It sets all wages by statute

questions.question: NEDLAC's four constituencies are:
options: Parliament, the courts, the Reserve Bank and Treasury
GOVERNMENT, organised BUSINESS, organised LABOUR and organised COMMUNITY

questions.question: NEDLAC's function is that:
options: Significant labour legislation and major economic policy are negotiated there BEFORE Parliament — social dialogue seeking consensus rather than imposition

questions.question: NEDLAC's honest limitation is:
options: It meets only once a decade
Consensus-seeking is slow, and constituencies that are not well organised are less well represented at the table

questions.question: The consistent macro-economic aims are:
options: Performance (growth), employment creation, equitable distribution, economic stability and external stability

questions.question: The permanent tension between the aims is that:
options: Redistribution needs revenue which needs growth; growth may need incentives favouring the advantaged; stability constrains borrowing for social spending

questions.question: Measurable achievements of redress include:
options: Expanded access to basic services, housing, education and grants; a substantial Black middle and professional class; shifted ownership and management demographics; and a body of protective law

questions.question: The critique that "broad-based" in B-BBEE responds to is:
options: That benefits sometimes concentrated among a narrow elite rather than spreading broadly

subtopics.title: Starting the Race at Different Lines

questions.question: The two matric candidates illustrate that:
options: Same exam and same effort can meet very different starting lines

questions.question: The starting lines came from:
options: LAWS deciding who could own land, where families could live, which schools got money, and who could hold which job

questions.question: "The law is equal now" and "the economy is equal now" differ because:
options: Repeal stopped the machine but did not undo what it built — transferred land, lost schooling and absent collateral persist
Equality is purely a legal concept

subtopics.title: Four Things You Need to Build a Livelihood

questions.question: "Land alone is a field, not a farm" means:
options: Without seed money, equipment, training and buyers, a title deed feeds nobody — transfer PLUS support, or the transfer fails

questions.question: Skills redress is funded and delivered through:
options: A skills levy funding learnerships, apprenticeships and trade training — building qualifications people were denied

questions.question: "Just start a business" is easy advice for someone with capital, contacts and a customer list, which is why entrepreneurship redress provides:
options: Incubators, simpler paperwork, procurement set-asides and mentorship

questions.question: The one test to apply to any redress instrument:
options: Does it hand over a THING, or does it build a working LIVELIHOOD?
Does it cost less than last year?
Was it copied from another country?

questions.question: A notice inviting public comment on a proposed tariff increase is an example of:
options: Public participation — regulators and lawmakers required to hear those affected before deciding

questions.question: NEDLAC is "deliberately slower than one minister deciding" because:
options: The people who will live with a policy argue about it before it becomes law — consensus over imposition

questions.question: Self-regulating bodies such as professional councils:
options: Set and police professional standards INSIDE a legal framework — decisions devolved to those who understand the work, with public accountability

questions.question: The fair way to judge redress is:
options: BOTH columns — real gains in services, housing, schooling, grants and a growing professional class; real shortfalls in unemployment, inequality, land reform pace and narrowly pooled benefits
Neither — the question is purely political
